records.table: From Hacienda La Caravedo in Ica, Pisco Portón Mosto Verde Acholado blends three Peruvian grapes, distilled once from must that has not finished fermenting and bottled at 43 per cent with no water added. In a Pisco Sour it brings flowers, ripe fruit and orange blossom.
records.story: Pisco is the grape brandy of Peru's southern coast, and Hacienda La Caravedo in the Ica valley dates its own distilling to 1684, a date the house gives and travel guides repeat. The Portón label was made there in modern times, named for the Spanish word for a gate. It was built on the old Peruvian rules: eight pisco grapes, one distillation, no water to bring the strength down and no wood. Its mosto verde, distilled from must before it finishes fermenting, was made in seven single grapes and in the acholado blend. In the United States the tequila Patrón, whose name sounds close to Portón to an English ear, challenged the brand, and the American registration of the Portón name was cancelled in 2017. The house withdrew the name from that market, and the same distillery's piscos came to American shelves as Caravedo, the distillery's own name. Its mosto verde gives a guest the Peruvian way in brief: a blend of grapes, one pass through the still, and a strength reached at the still.

records.table: BarSol Primero Quebranta is a pisco of one grape, Quebranta, distilled once in copper pot stills at Bodega San Isidro in Ica and bottled at 41.3 per cent, the strength it came off the still. Pear, red apple and fresh grass on the nose sit over the body Quebranta gives.
records.story: Bodega San Isidro stands in the Ica valley, on Peru's southern coast, and it is older than the label it makes: the house calls it a century old distillery, and the Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails notes evidence of pisco made there in the nineteenth century. It had lain idle since 1968 when a group of investors based in the United States bought it in 2002 and brought it back to work, reconditioning the old buildings and keeping to the pot still method that, as the house tells it, Peru has followed since the sixteenth century. They called the pisco BarSol, for the sun of Ica and the bars of the world, in the house's telling, and by 2005 it was going abroad, first among its range the pure Quebranta named Primero. The range grew to cover every style Peru's rules allow: puros of single grapes, an acholado that blends them, and mosto verde distilled from must before its fermentation ends. Newer labels print the pure Quebranta as BarSol Puro Quebranta, at the same strength. Pour it when a guest asks what Quebranta tastes like: the non aromatic grape that gives Peruvian pisco its body, in a pisco made for the Pisco Sour.

records.story: Macchu Pisco was founded in 2006 by two sisters who came home to Peru to build a label for Peruvian pisco made in the traditional way. Peru had made pisco its denomination of origin in 1990, binding it to the grapes, the single distillation and the rest without wood. The name plays on Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel, spelt with a double c. The house began with Quebranta, the non aromatic grape that gives Peruvian pisco its earthy body, distilled once in copper pot stills in the valley of Ica and rested a year, by the house's account, in vessels that give it nothing, before it is bottled at the estate. Two other bottlings show the other two Peruvian styles: La Diablada, an acholado named for an Andean dance in which angels fight devils, and Ñusta, a mosto verde named for the Quechua word for an Inca princess. Set beside an Italia or a Torontel pisco, the plain bottle shows what Quebranta brings: pepper, citrus and earth where the aromatic grapes give flowers.

records.story: Chile gave pisco a denomination of origin in 1931, reserving the name for the grape spirit of its northern regions of Atacama and Coquimbo. Seven years later, in February 1938, twenty-five growers of the Elqui Valley joined together at Paihuano in a society that became a cooperative, its legal standing granted in 1939. Its name, Capel, is made of the initials of Cooperativa Agrícola Pisquera Elqui. By the cooperative's account it later bought a distillery at Vicuña, in the Elqui Valley, which became its plant there, and it went on to take in growers from across both pisco regions. In 1999 a decree set Chile's grades of pisco by strength: Corriente from 30 per cent, Especial from 35, Reservado from 40 and Gran Pisco from 43. Chilean pisco may also be distilled more than once, brought down with water and rested in wood, and Capel's Reservado is distilled twice, as its label says. Capel is the name that stands for Chilean pisco, and its Reservado teaches a guest that Chile grades pisco by strength, not by age.

records.story: The Torres family of Penedès, in Catalonia, began distilling wine into brandy in 1928. In 1979 the family founded Miguel Torres Chile in the Curicó Valley, among the first foreign wine companies to settle in Chile. Its pisco came, by the house's own account, in 2012, eighty-four years after that first still in Penedès: Moscatel grapes from the Limarí Valley, in the Coquimbo region, distilled once in copper to keep their perfume. The name, the Governor, honours a man who fought for Chilean independence at the Battle of Maipú in 1818 and was later made governor of Ovalle, the town of the valley. The bottle entered a spirit that two countries claim. Chile reserves the name pisco to its Atacama and Coquimbo regions and allows more than one distillation, water and wood; Peru allows none of the three. El Gobernador keeps to a single distillation, as Peru does, and stays Chilean in its region and its grade, Reservado, a strength of 40 per cent. Muscat flowers in a clear spirit of the Reservado grade: in this bottle a guest meets aromatic Chilean pisco.

traps: El Gobernador is Chilean, not Peruvian: a guest who asks for a Peruvian pisco wants another bottle.
Reservado on the label is a strength, 40 per cent, not an age: El Gobernador is clear and has never seen wood.
It is made in Chile, by the Chilean house of Miguel Torres, not in Spain: the grapes and the stills are in the Limarí Valley.

cards.prompt: Which grapes make El Gobernador Pisco?
cards.answer: Moscatel of Alexandria and pink Moscatel of the Limarí Valley, in roughly equal parts.

cards.prompt: Who is the governor of El Gobernador?
cards.answer: A patriot who fought at Maipú in 1818 and was later made governor of Ovalle, the town of the Limarí Valley.

quiz.q: A guest asks why El Gobernador smells of roses and jasmine. Which grapes is it made from?
quiz.explain: It is made from Moscatel of Alexandria and pink Moscatel, aromatic grapes that carry the perfume; Pedro Jiménez is the neutral grape of Capel's clear Reservado.

quiz.q: Which town did the man honoured by El Gobernador's name later govern?
quiz.explain: He fought at Maipú in 1818 and was later made governor of Ovalle, the town of the Limarí Valley; Vicuña lies in the Elqui Valley, where Capel works.

report: The bottle's grapes, still, rest, strength, taste, pour and the governor's story are the liquor shelf's El Gobernador record, a reviewed page of this repo, reworded; the Torres pages read confirm the grapes, the single distillation and the 40 per cent Reservado grade.

The launch year 2012 is the house's own (eighty-four years after 1928, on the Torres and Miguel Torres Chile pages) and is told as the house's account; the year field stays empty because no independent source dated the launch. A gold medal of 2013 on the house's page shows the bottle existed by then, and is not carried under the voice rule.

The governor is described, not named: the shelf names him (Felipe Margutt Donaire), but his dates were not found in two sources, so the brief's rule for the dead keeps his name out of this record. The shelf's own line names him without dates; the integrator may want to look at it.

Miguel Torres Chile's founding in 1979 in the Curicó Valley rests on the Torres page and Wikipedia. Among the first foreign wine companies is the cautious wording; Wikipedia and others say the first foreign winery, which is left out as a claim of a first.

The Torres family member who created the pisco is living and named nowhere; Miguel Torres Maczassek and Miguel A. Torres already stand in people.json. Juan Torres Casals (1865 to 1932 on the house's blog) is described as the family, since his dates stand in one source only.
Torres 10 in others rests on the Torres page for that brandy: Penedès, American oak and the solera method; its age is not stated and is not given.

open: story: the governor's own dates were not found (a museum paper of 2026 places him among two former officers of Napoleon serving Ovalle from 1831 to 1848, and a Swedish listing makes him governor in 1843); he stays described, not named.
